problem.title: Eliminating Alert Fatigue with SLO Burn-Rate Alerts
problem.prompt: Your payments platform processes 12,000 RPS across 180 Kubernetes pods. Over the past quarter, on-call SREs averaged 420 PagerDuty pages per week (60/day), 88% of which self-resolved within 3 minutes without customer impact. Last Tuesday, a real 22-minute P1 database connection-pool exhaustion in checkout-service was buried under 47 downstream timeout pages and auto-acknowledged by an exhausted engineer. Redesign the alerting and paging pipeline so only actionable, user-impacting incidents wake on-call engineers while preserving observability for transient anomalies.

spark.summary: On-call engineers receive 400+ PagerDuty pages per week from transient 5xx spikes and single-pod CPU bursts, leading to blind acknowledgments and a missed 22-minute P1 checkout outage.
spark.keyTakeaway: Replace symptom-based infrastructure thresholds with multi-window SLO burn-rate alerts, Alertmanager inhibition/grouping, and deterministic dedup_key routing.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Across 180 Kubernetes pods serving `12,000 RPS`, paging on raw infrastructure thresholds (CPU > 80%, brief 5xx blips) generated `420` PagerDuty pages per week—`88%` of which self-resolved in under 3 minutes.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 420 Weekly Noise Pages vs. Multi-Window SLO Routing (Prometheus HA -> Alertmanager -> PagerDuty); Error Budget Burn Rate Escalation Tiers (HEALTHY (<1x) -> SLOW BURN (1-6x) -> FAST BURN (14.4x)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Alerting on a single short window (e.g., `5m error > 1%`) still pages on brief self-healing blips; alerting on a single long window (e.g., `1h error > 1%`) either takes too long. Error-budget alerting is the standard SRE operating model for high-scale services: **Payments & Checkout APIs**: Pages only when customer-visible availability or latency SLOs burn dangerously fast.

learningJourney.title: Alert fatigue, cascade storms, and duplicate HA pages
learningJourney.explanation:
Three alerting anti-patterns compound during real incidents:

1. **Noise Habituation**: 60 pages/day train responders to blindly acknowledge notifications.
2. **Downstream Cascade Flood**: One Postgres failure fires 47 gateway/upstream `504` pages simultaneously.
3. **HA Pair Duplicates**: Active-active Prometheus pairs page twice without deterministic `dedup_key` routing.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Multi-Window Burn Rates, Inhibition, and Dedup Keys
learningJourney.explanation:
Cut weekly pages from `420` to `< 15` while keeping P1 MTTD `<= 2 minutes`:

- **Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Rules (99.9% SLO -> `0.001` budget)**: Page immediately on `14.4x` burn (`2%` of 30-day budget in 1h) **only when BOTH** `1h` AND `5m` windows exceed `14.4 * 0.001`—catching hard drops in `<= 2m` while resetting fast on recovery.
- **Slow-Burn Ticket Tier**: Route `1x–3x` burn (`6h` & `30m`, or `3d` & `6h`) to Slack/Jira tickets instead of PagerDuty.
- **Alertmanager Grouping & `inhibit_rules`**: Group by `(cluster, service)` with `group_wait: 30s`, `group_interval: 5m`, inhibit downstream `504` pages when root-cause `PostgresCritical` fires, and hash `(alertname, cluster, service)` into PagerDuty `dedup_key`.

sectionDiagram.title: Error Budget Burn Rate Escalation Tiers
sectionDiagram.summary: Requiring both long and short windows to breach eliminates blip noise and clears pages immediately upon recovery.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
groups:
  - name: checkout_slo_burn_rate
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:error_ratio5m
        expr: |
          sum by (cluster, service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          / sum by (cluster, service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
      - alert: CheckoutSLOBurnRateCritical
        expr: |
          job:http_requests:error_ratio1h{service="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          job:http_requests:error_ratio5m{service="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
```

learningJourney.title: Where SLO burn-rate alerting governs production reliability
learningJourney.explanation:
Error-budget alerting is the standard SRE operating model for high-scale services:

- **Payments & Checkout APIs**: Pages only when customer-visible availability or latency SLOs burn dangerously fast.
- **Automated Canary Rollbacks**: Uses the same `5m` burn-rate recording rules to abort bad deployments.
- **Multi-Region HA Observability**: Uses Alertmanager `dedup_key` and `inhibit_rules` across redundant Prometheus pairs.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does Google SRE multi-window burn-rate alerting require BOTH a long window (e.g., 1h) AND a short window (e.g., 5m) to exceed the burn threshold before paging?

options.text: The 1h window filters out brief self-healing blips while the 5m window ensures the outage is still actively burning budget right now
options.feedback: Correct: pairing long and short windows prevents both false pages on short spikes and slow reset lag after recovery.

options.feedback: Prometheus can evaluate 5m windows, but single-window rules either over-page or reset slowly.

options.feedback: The dual-window check happens inside the PromQL alert rule.

_nextProblem.title: Solving Dual-Write Cache Invalidation Races
_nextProblem.prompt: Your user profile service uses classic Cache-Aside against PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7 (30,000 reads/sec, 800 writes/sec). Writers execute `UPDATE profiles ...` followed by `redis.del(key)`. Readers on a cache miss execute `SELECT ...` and then `redis.set(key, val, ex=3600)`. Under concurrent load, ~0.05% of profile updates (~35/day) revert to old values in Redis for up to 1 hour because a concurrent cache-miss reader fetched `v1` before the writer committed `v2`, paused on GC/network, and wrote `v1` into Redis after the writer's `DEL`. Redesign the read/write caching protocol to make stale cache repopulation impossible.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
